Ada Mason was his accomplice: her account of seeing a man in Ruth's compartment was designed to point toward the Comte de la Roche, and her description could be adjusted as the investigation required. Knighton killed Ruth on the train and took the Heart of Fire, while the count's planned meeting and Derek's presence supplied convenient alternative suspects. Poirot uses Papopolous's knowledge of the jewel trade, Knighton's handling of evidence, and pressure on Mason to break the prepared story. The ruby is recovered and the count's fraud exposed, though he is not the killer. Derek is cleared of Ruth's murder. Mirelle's attempt to hold him with incriminating claims fails, and his attachment to Katherine becomes plain. Knighton's courtship of Katherine is revealed as part concealment and part miscalculation; Katherine survives the case and is free to choose a future with Derek.
recaps.in_short: Rufus Van Aldin gives his estranged daughter Ruth Kettering the Heart of Fire, a famous ruby, before she takes the Blue Train to the Riviera. Ruth plans to meet her lover, the Comte de la Roche, while her impecunious husband Derek and the dancer Mirelle complicate her private life. On the journey Ruth befriends Katherine Grey, newly wealthy after years as a companion. Ruth is found murdered in her compartment and the ruby is gone. Poirot investigates at Van Aldin's request, testing the evidence of Ruth's maid Ada Mason, the count's schemes, Derek's movements, and Mirelle's jealousy. He discovers that Van Aldin's trusted secretary, Major Richard Knighton, is the international thief known as the Marquis. Knighton killed Ruth for the ruby, aided by Mason, whose story about a man in the compartment was manufactured to misdirect the inquiry. Knighton is exposed, Derek is cleared, and Katherine emerges from the case with the prospect of a life with Derek rather than the cautious isolation she expected.

recaps.text: American financier Rufus Van Aldin purchases the Heart of Fire, a celebrated ruby, and gives it to his daughter Ruth Kettering. Ruth is separated from her charming but penniless husband Derek, and Van Aldin urges her to complete the divorce. He is equally alarmed by her renewed connection with the Comte de la Roche, a polished adventurer who knows about the jewel. Van Aldin's trusted secretary, Major Richard Knighton, manages the arrangements. Elsewhere, Katherine Grey finishes years of service as companion to a difficult old woman and unexpectedly inherits a fortune. She decides to travel, entering a world in which her good sense is more reliable than her new money.

Katherine boards the Blue Train for the Riviera and falls into conversation with Ruth, who hints at an unhappy marriage and an important decision. In Paris Ruth dismisses her maid, Ada Mason, for the night. The next day Ruth is found dead in her compartment, her face badly injured and the Heart of Fire missing. Mason says a man was with Ruth in Paris but that she did not see him clearly. The known appointment with the Comte de la Roche immediately directs suspicion toward him. Derek Kettering has also been travelling in the region, and Ruth's death gives him a financial interest as her husband. Poirot, another passenger, agrees to help Van Aldin while the French authorities begin their inquiry.

At the Riviera Poirot compares the accounts of the train journey with the relationships surrounding Ruth. Katherine stays with her cousin Lady Rosalie Tamplin and Rosalie's sharp-eyed daughter Lenox, placing her near Derek and his lover Mirelle. Derek admits enough to look reckless but denies killing Ruth; Mirelle is jealous of the ease between him and Katherine. The count's interest in Ruth's jewels is real, yet Poirot doubts that his familiar form of fraud explains every feature of the murder. Mason's evidence remains central because it supplies the unknown man in Ruth's compartment, but her inability to identify him makes the story unusually convenient. Knighton assists Van Aldin and grows close to Katherine while Poirot quietly checks what each person knew about the ruby.

Poirot follows the jewel rather than the most visible romance. In Paris he consults Demetrius Papopolous, an old contact with detailed knowledge of stolen gems, and learns more about the international thief called the Marquis. The Heart of Fire is valuable enough to draw a professional scheme, and the mutilation of Ruth's face may have been meant to confuse identification as well as to show violence. The count can be tied to an attempt to profit from Ruth, but evidence against him does not account cleanly for the timing aboard the train. Poirot also studies Mason's prepared recollection, Derek's movements, Mirelle's changing statements, and the access enjoyed by people in Van Aldin's confidence. Katherine remains important because Ruth spoke to her without knowing her and because Katherine notices character without trying to build a case.

The inquiry narrows as Poirot separates several genuine deceptions from the murder itself. The Comte de la Roche has lied and schemed for the ruby, but his dishonesty is too obvious to settle the case. Mirelle tries to use what she knows of Derek's movements to keep control of him, while Derek's feelings for Katherine become harder to disguise. Poirot returns repeatedly to the information available before the journey: who knew Van Aldin had bought the Heart of Fire, who knew Ruth would carry it, and who could arrange testimony inside the sleeping car. Papopolous's information about the Marquis suggests that the robbery was not an impulsive act. Poirot applies pressure to the witness whose account created the apparent stranger in Ruth's compartment and prepares to confront the person behind it.

Poirot exposes Major Richard Knighton as Ruth Kettering's murderer and as the master jewel thief known as the Marquis. Knighton's place beside Van Aldin gave him advance knowledge of the Heart of Fire and Ruth's journey. Ada Mason was his accomplice, and her report of an indistinct man in Ruth's compartment was constructed to direct attention toward the Comte de la Roche while remaining flexible enough to survive questioning. Knighton killed Ruth aboard the train and stole the ruby, using the count's plans, Derek's financial interest, and Mirelle's jealousy as layers of misdirection. Poirot's inquiries through Papopolous connect the professional theft to the supposedly respectable secretary, and Mason's story fails under pressure. The ruby is recovered, Derek is cleared, and Knighton's interest in Katherine is stripped of its reassuring appearance. Katherine comes through the case independently wealthy and emotionally changed, with Derek now free and the possibility of a future between them.

characters.description: A young reporter for L'Epoque whose round face, intense curiosity, and stubborn reliance on reason make him seem older than his years. He treats the apparently impossible assault at the Chateau du Glandier as a problem of facts rather than the supernatural and insists that the evidence must be made to fit a coherent explanation.
characters.name: Joseph Rouletabille

characters.description: A lawyer and friend of Rouletabille who narrates the investigation. Sainclair accompanies the reporter to the Glandier, records conversations and evidence, and often shares the reader's bewilderment while Rouletabille keeps parts of his reasoning private.
characters.name: Sainclair

characters.description: The daughter and scientific collaborator of Professor Stangerson. She is found gravely injured inside the locked Yellow Room after cries for help bring the household running. Her reluctance to explain what happened makes the physical mystery inseparable from a private one.
characters.name: Mathilde Stangerson

characters.description: A respected scientist who lives and works at the Chateau du Glandier with his daughter Mathilde. He is devoted to her and is among the first people to force entry into the Yellow Room after hearing her struggle within.
characters.name: Professor Stangerson

characters.description: Professor Stangerson's long-serving laboratory assistant. Father Jacques is near the Yellow Room when Mathilde cries out and helps break through its locked door, making him an important witness to the room's sealed condition.
characters.name: Father Jacques

characters.description: Mathilde Stangerson's devoted suitor, whose long courtship has finally gained her acceptance. His guarded behavior and unexplained absences trouble the official investigators, although Rouletabille remains wary of conclusions built from appearances.
characters.name: Robert Darzac

characters.description: A celebrated police detective brought into the Yellow Room case. Larsan is methodical, confident, and widely admired, but he and Rouletabille differ sharply over how the clues should be interpreted and whom they implicate.
characters.name: Frederic Larsan

characters.description: The examining magistrate assigned to the assault on Mathilde Stangerson. He conducts formal questioning at the chateau and initially regards the young reporter's interventions with a mixture of impatience and curiosity.
characters.name: M. de Marquet

characters.description: The concierge of the Chateau du Glandier. He and his wife occupy the lodge and become part of the inquiry because movements through the estate, and the testimony of everyone guarding its approaches, matter to the reconstruction of the crime.
characters.name: Mr. Bernier

characters.description: The concierge's wife at the Chateau du Glandier. Her position at the lodge makes her one of the household witnesses questioned about who could have entered or left the grounds around the attacks.
characters.name: Mrs. Bernier

characters.description: The Stangerson estate's gamekeeper, nicknamed for his green clothing and outdoor duties. His movements in the woods and his relations with members of the household draw Rouletabille's attention as the danger at the Glandier continues.
characters.name: The Gamekeeper

characters.description: An American acquaintance of the Stangersons who is staying near the Glandier. He takes an interest in the case and has knowledge of Mathilde from years before, giving him a perspective that reaches beyond the immediate household.
characters.name: Arthur Rance

recaps.ending: Rouletabille returns in time for Robert Darzac's trial and identifies the supposed detective Frederic Larsan as Ballmeyer, a criminal and master of disguise. Years earlier Ballmeyer had deceived Mathilde into a secret marriage in America under another name. Because he was still alive, she could not marry Darzac without exposing her past, and Ballmeyer used that secret to terrorize her. The first locked-room puzzle resulted from a gap between the original assault and the alarm: Mathilde, later alone, relived the violence in a nightmare and reopened her injury, so no attacker had to escape the sealed room then. During the later gallery attack, Ballmeyer only seemed to join the pursuit as Larsan because the pursuer and fugitive were the same man. Given time to recognize the danger, Ballmeyer escapes before he can be arrested. Darzac is cleared, while Rouletabille keeps the most personal part of Mathilde's history private.
recaps.in_short: After Mathilde Stangerson is nearly killed inside a bedroom whose locked door and barred window offer no escape, young reporter Joseph Rouletabille investigates at the Chateau du Glandier. He competes with famous detective Frederic Larsan, whose reading of the clues increasingly points toward Mathilde's fiance, Robert Darzac. A second attack produces another impossible disappearance, and Darzac's secrecy leads to his arrest. At trial, Rouletabille proves that Larsan is really Ballmeyer, a disguised criminal who had deceived Mathilde into a secret marriage years earlier and was blackmailing and attacking her. The Yellow Room seemed impossible because the household responded not to the original attack but to Mathilde's later nightmare and accidental reopening of her wound; the assailant had already left. In the gallery, Ballmeyer escaped by resuming his identity as the detective who appeared to be chasing him. Darzac is exonerated, but Ballmeyer escapes, and Rouletabille withholds the personal secret that helped him understand Mathilde.

recaps.text: News reaches Paris that Mathilde Stangerson has been brutally attacked in the Yellow Room, a chamber adjoining her father's laboratory at the Chateau du Glandier. Professor Stangerson and Father Jacques heard her cries and the sounds of a struggle, but the door was locked from within and the window was secured. When they broke in, Mathilde lay badly wounded while her attacker had vanished. A bloody handprint, footprints, a weapon, and signs of gunfire suggest a real intruder, yet the room appears to allow no exit. Sainclair, a lawyer, discusses the case with his young reporter friend Joseph Rouletabille. Rouletabille rejects supernatural explanations and travels with Sainclair to the Glandier, convinced that the apparently contradictory evidence can be reconciled.

At the chateau, Rouletabille examines the room, the laboratory, the grounds, and the testimony of the household. He meets Robert Darzac, Mathilde's fiance, and Frederic Larsan, the famous police detective known as the Great Fred. Larsan's authority does not prevent Rouletabille from challenging his assumptions. The official inquiry focuses on physical traces and on whether anyone in or near the household is concealing a route or an accomplice. Mathilde survives but cannot or will not give a full account of her attacker. Rouletabille becomes convinced that her silence is deliberate and that the case cannot be solved without understanding why she protects a secret even after nearly being killed.

Rouletabille remains at the Glandier as Mathilde recovers, arranging observations and testing the movements possible through the chateau. Suspicion begins to settle around Darzac: his conduct is evasive, his whereabouts cannot always be satisfactorily explained, and he refuses to defend himself by revealing what he knows. Rouletabille nevertheless resists treating secrecy as proof of guilt. The reporter prepares for another attack, believing that the unknown enemy remains close and that Mathilde is still in danger. His investigation increasingly becomes a contest with Larsan, whose orderly case against an obvious suspect conflicts with Rouletabille's insistence that some central fact has been misunderstood.

Despite the watch placed around Mathilde, an assailant reaches her again. Rouletabille and the others pursue a fleeing figure through the gallery, covering the available exits, yet the man seems to disappear from a space with no unguarded way out. The new impossibility deepens the mystery rather than resolving the first one. The estate's gamekeeper is also found dead, linking the violence inside the chateau with secret nighttime movements in the grounds. Mathilde's terror and continued silence leave Darzac exposed, while Rouletabille studies the exact positions and timing of every pursuer. He believes the gallery puzzle is based on a mistaken identity rather than an impossible escape.

The accumulating circumstantial evidence leads to Darzac's arrest. He still refuses to disclose the private matter that could explain his actions, and Mathilde cannot save him without revealing the same secret. Rouletabille distinguishes between the evidence that places Darzac under suspicion and the deeper pattern connecting both attacks. He concludes that the mystery contains two overlapping trails: one created by the true criminal and another produced by innocent efforts to hide Mathilde's past. Certain of the culprit's identity but needing proof and additional information, Rouletabille leaves on a journey while Darzac's case advances toward trial.

Rouletabille arrives at Darzac's trial and overturns the prosecution's case. Frederic Larsan is actually Ballmeyer, a wanted criminal adept at disguises. In America years earlier he had used another identity to deceive Mathilde into a secret marriage; his survival prevented her from marrying Darzac and let him threaten her into silence. In the Yellow Room, the household's midnight alarm did not mark the time of the original attack. After Ballmeyer had gone, Mathilde relived the assault in a nightmare and struck and reopened her wound, creating the false impression that an assailant had just escaped a sealed room. In the gallery, Ballmeyer vanished by changing from the pursued man back into Larsan, one of the apparent pursuers. Rouletabille's demonstration clears Darzac. Ballmeyer has already fled, however, having recognized the trap, and Rouletabille does not expose more of Mathilde's private history than the case requires.
